samplingProtocol: The drone (DJI MavicPro2) was deployed when weather conditions allowed (wind velocity <10 kts, good visibility). Aerial survey imagery consisted in flying the drone at high altitude (approximately 500 m) and manually taking high-resolution images of the general setup of the working area. Mapping operations consisted in flying the drone along a pre-programmed automated flight path at an altitude of approximately 60 m, resulting in a sequence of georeferenced images suitable for orthomosaic and photogrammetric processing.

Images of the sea floor were collected using a Remotely Operated Vehicle (BlueROV2) equipped with cameras and onboard sensors. The ROV was flown at constant speed (>1 m s⁻¹) and approximately constant altitude (around 1 m above the seabed, depending on visibility). Sampling consisted of flying the ROV over predefined square-shaped areas or along transects to document benthic habitats.

Vertical salinity and temperature profiles were performed using ODDI sensors for depth, salinity and temperature, together with a HOBO light sensor. The sensor was conditioned in cold seawater prior to deployment, held briefly at the surface, and then lowered slowly through the water column from the surface to near-bottom.

A Bombard C4 inflatable tender was used to access shallow or restricted areas where the main vessel could not operate. The tender supported scouting, bathymetric surveys and deployment or recovery of scientific gear.

Scientific SCUBA diving was used to conduct underwater observations and sampling as part of the site characterisation and sampling strategy. Divers operated in shallow coastal areas to document habitats and carry out sampling tasks.

Water sampling was carried out using a General Oceanic Niskin bottle deployed at a discrete depth in the water column, including surface, intermediate depths or approximately 1 m above the seabed. Niskin sampling was used in combination with CTD profiling or as a standalone water collection event.

Baited amphipod traps (AT) were used to capture scavenging communities present in the area. The custom traps were composed of a coarse plastic mesh protecting a 500 µm fine mesh rolled around two PVC rings to produce a 15 × 40 cm cylinder. Both ends of the trap were equipped with inward-facing funnels (2 cm opening) to prevent organisms from escaping. Fresh mackerel and squid enclosed in a fine mesh tea-bag were used as bait. Traps were deployed in pairs, secured together with a metal frame, anchored with a 5 kg ballast weight, and connected to a surface buoy. Deployment duration ranged from 24 to 36 hours.

A special effort was devoted to generate fine-scale bathymetric charts for sampling areas before and during sampling operations. Bathymetric charts were generated using the ReefMaster v2.0 software based on data collected with the RV Australis onboard single-beam echosounder (Furuno FCV 295) and a portable echosounder (Humminbird Helix 5) mounted on the Bombard C4 tender for shallow areas.

In total, CTD profiles were taken at multiple locations to characterise the water column. Vertical temperature and salinity profiles were obtained by lowering CTD sensors through the water column from the surface to near-bottom.

Cyanobacteria sampling targeted colored ice and biofilms covering intertidal rocks. Intertidal rock biofilms were collected using disinfected metal tools and stored in sterile containers, while colored ice patches were sawed and stored in clean bags. Samples were preserved and stored frozen shortly after collection.

Sea ice work was designed to complement the sampling strategy of the water column. Two drifting ice floes were sampled near the main study sites. Sampling included the collection of ice cores, microlayer samples and under-ice seawater to capture physical, biological and biogeochemical parameters.
Intertidal zones were visited to collect biological material, including biofilms and associated organisms, and to document environmental conditions in shallow coastal habitats.

Benthic sampling was carried out using a Rauschert dredge composed of a sledge-like metal frame dragging a mesh bag protected by rubber carpets along the seafloor to collect benthic and megabenthic organisms.
Soft-bottom sediment samples were collected using a Van Veen grab to estimate the abundance and biomass of macrobenthic infauna. Collected sediments were sieved on a 1 mm mesh to retain organisms.

Sediment traps were deployed on the seafloor and recovered after the deployment period. Each sediment trap consisted of a funnel connected to a sampling bottle filled with preservative solution to collect sinking particulate material.
